name: Septoplasty

card.summary: Functional surgery that straightens a deviated nasal septum to improve breathing; it is not a cosmetic nose reshaping, though the two are often combined.
card.note: Evidence supports symptom relief for obstruction; it is a breathing operation and is distinguished from rhinoplasty, which changes external appearance.

quick.overview:
Septoplasty is an operation that straightens the nasal septum, the wall of cartilage and bone between the two nostrils, when it is bent enough to block airflow. It is done through the nostrils, usually as an outpatient procedure.

It is primarily a functional surgery. In looksmaxxing forums it comes up because people with a crooked septum ask whether it will change how the nose looks, or whether it should be combined with rhinoplasty or jaw surgery.
quick.mechanism: The surgeon makes an incision in the lining of the septum, then removes or repositions deviated bone and cartilage while keeping enough for support. Splints, sutures or grafts may be used afterward. Because the incisions are inside the nose, there is generally no external scar, and the external shape is not the goal.
quick.risks: Reported risks include bleeding, septal perforation, septal haematoma, reduced sense of smell, temporary numbness of the front upper teeth, and, less often, a dropped nasal tip or saddle deformity from over-resection. Symptoms can persist or recur in some patients. Procedures on the turbinates carry their own discussed risks, such as empty nose syndrome.

lead: Septoplasty is a surgical procedure that straightens a deviated nasal septum, the partition of cartilage and bone between the two nasal cavities, to relieve obstruction.[1][2] It is also called septal reconstruction or submucous septal resection.[1] It is performed through the nostrils, under local or general anaesthesia, and most operations take about an hour or less according to Wikipedia.[1] People who care about how their nose looks come to it from two directions: a crooked septum can sit beneath a crooked-looking nose, and the septum is the usual source of cartilage that rhinoplasty surgeons use to rebuild and support the nose, so septal and cosmetic surgery are often planned together as septorhinoplasty.[2][9][17]

Its main indications are nasal obstruction, recurrent nosebleeds from a septal spur, and associated rhinitis or sinus problems.[1] The condition it treats is common: Wikipedia states that some septal displacement affects about 80 percent of people, usually unnoticed, and a 2022 narrative review calls minor asymptomatic deviation a normal developmental variation.[16][18] A multicentre prospective study of adults with septal deviation and symptomatic obstruction, the NOSE study, found improved disease-specific quality of life after septoplasty, and a 2023 randomised trial published in the BMJ found greater improvement in symptoms at six months after septoplasty than with nasal sprays alone.[1][3][20]

Septoplasty is distinct from rhinoplasty, which reshapes the external nose. Wikipedia's article on deviated septum says septoplasty itself causes no cosmetic change and leaves no external scar, while listing external deformity as a possible complication.[16] In looksmaxxing forums it is discussed mainly as a breathing operation that members ask about in relation to nose appearance, rhinoplasty and jaw surgery.[4][5][6]

sections.h: Anatomy and why the septum matters for appearance
paras: The septum divides the nose into two passages. Its front part is cartilage and its back part is bone and thin cartilage, and the cartilage supports the nasal dorsum and tip.[2][16] Wikipedia lists uneven septal growth as the most common cause of deviation, with congenital deviation, age-related worsening and trauma such as childbirth or a broken nose as others; deviation is also linked to connective-tissue conditions such as Marfan syndrome and Ehlers-Danlos syndrome.[16] Symptoms it describes include blocked breathing, snoring, sinus infections, nosebleeds, mouth breathing and reduced smell.[16]

For appearance, the relevant points are that a bent septum can push the dorsum or tip off-centre, and that the cartilage in the septum is the preferred graft material in rhinoplasty. Wikipedia's rhinoplasty article says autologous grafts are usually taken from the septum and that rib or ear cartilage is used when septal cartilage is insufficient, which is common in revision surgery.[17] A 2014 review on children's noses notes that early surgery on the septum before growth is complete can affect later nasal development and function, so surgeons approach it cautiously in young patients.[2][21]

Septoplasty is used for airway obstruction that causes breathing difficulty, recurrent rhinitis or sinusitis, and for recurrent epistaxis caused by a septal spur.[1] Grokipedia adds that it is typically considered when conservative measures such as nasal sprays and decongestants have not relieved symptoms.[2] The NOSE study enrolled adults with septal deviation and obstruction lasting at least three months in whom medical management had failed.[3]
A deviated septum in some degree is common, and Grokipedia reports estimates that it affects a large proportion of the population, most of them mildly and without symptoms.[2]

The surgeon accesses the septum through the nostrils, incises the lining, and removes or realigns part of the bone or cartilage while preserving enough for structural support. The approach may be endoscopic or open, and splints, sutures or internal grafts may be used.[1] There are no external incisions in the usual approach.[2]

The procedure may be combined with turbinate surgery, sinus surgery, or rhinoplasty. A US survey of ambulatory sinonasal surgery grouped septoplasty and turbinate surgery as one of the most common categories of such operations.[7] A plastic-surgery study examined the relative importance of septal and nasal-valve surgery in correcting airway obstruction in primary and secondary rhinoplasty.[8]

Septal surgery has older roots than modern cosmetic rhinoplasty. Wikipedia's rhinoplasty article credits Freer (1902) and Killian (1904) with pioneering submucous resection, the operation that removed deviated septal tissue through the nose, and names Maurice Cottle in 1947 as an advocate of conserving the septum through a hemitransfixion incision and favouring closed surgery.[17] John Orlando Roe performed what Wikipedia calls the first modern endonasal rhinoplasty in 1887, and Jacques Joseph described nose reduction through internal incisions in 1928.[17]

Modern septoplasty emphasises preserving enough cartilage and bone for support rather than removing the septum, and endoscopic approaches are now compared with the conventional headlight technique in trials.[1][11][12] Wikipedia lists a multicentre randomised trial by Carrie and colleagues, published in the BMJ in October 2023, comparing septoplasty with medical management for nasal airway obstruction.[1][20]

External swelling or bruising is usually minimal. Internal splints are often removed 7 to 10 days after surgery, and tissues generally stabilise over 3 to 6 months, with some shifting possible for over a year.[1]

Wikipedia lists excessive bleeding (about 1% of patients), septal perforation, septal haematoma, reduced smell, temporary numbness of the upper front teeth, a dropped nasal tip, empty nose syndrome, septal abscess, adhesions and saddle nose from over-resection as possible complications. It lists acute infection, untreated diabetes, severe hypertension and bleeding disorders as contraindications.[1] Grokipedia reports that revision surgery may be needed in some patients and that obstruction can recur over years.[2]

A 2025 review of septal deviation describes septoplasty as generally safe and as improving quality of life for most patients, while noting that recurrence of symptoms is not uncommon and that careful patient selection and preoperative assessment shape outcomes.[19]

Because the cartilaginous septum supports the nasal tip and dorsum, surgery on it can influence nasal structure, and septal cartilage is often harvested for grafting in rhinoplasty.[2][9][17] Surgeons' technique papers, such as a 10-year experience with the tongue-in-groove technique in septorhinoplasty, address combining septal and cosmetic work.[9] A purely functional septoplasty is not intended to change the external shape.[2][16]

Wikipedia's rhinoplasty article distinguishes functional rhinoplasty, which relieves obstruction and typically includes septoplasty, turbinate reduction and spreader grafts, from cosmetic rhinoplasty performed for aesthetic reasons.[17] It reports that revision rhinoplasty is needed in roughly 5 to 20 percent of operations and that swelling can take at least a year to resolve fully.[17] A plastic-surgery study found septal correction and nasal-valve surgery both important to airway improvement in primary and secondary rhinoplasty.[8]

Public interest in nose appearance is high on social media. Wikipedia notes that a TikTok trend called NoseJobCheck, in which people posted before-and-after rhinoplasty videos in early 2021, drew over a billion views of the hashtag.[17]

On looksmax.org, users post about scheduling septoplasty for breathing reasons and asking whether surgeons will also adjust the nasal tip during an insurance-covered operation.[4] One poster who is planning septoplasty for breathing asks whether to add rhinoplasty or wait for bimaxillary jaw surgery, which they believe can reduce the apparent size of a large nose.[5] Other threads ask whether it is acceptable to have septoplasty before bimax and how recovery felt.[6]

A separate thread compares turbinate reduction with other options, with some users warning about empty nose syndrome and others saying turbinate reduction is the only fix for true turbinate obstruction.[10] On T Nation, a member who had septoplasty and turbinate reduction for sleep apnea says he would not recommend it, and another thread asks when heavy lifting can resume after septoplasty.[22][23]

A registered randomised trial of functional nasal surgery performed at the time of Le Fort I jaw surgery reflects the same overlap between breathing surgery and jaw surgery that forum members discuss; its results are not described in the registry entry.[24]

The NOSE study, a prospective multicentre observational study, assessed disease-specific quality of life after septoplasty in adults with nasal obstruction and reported improvement.[3] A 2023 BMJ randomised trial reported greater improvement in symptoms and quality of life at six months after septoplasty than with nasal-spray management.[1]

Registered trials include comparisons of conventional versus endoscopic septoplasty,[11][12] a trial of septoplasty with or without inferior turbinate reduction,[13] a study of silastic sheets after septoplasty,[14] and a trial of septoplasty's effect on headache that was recruiting at the time of the registry listing.[15] Results of several of these registrations are not described in the registry entries.
Reviews describe septoplasty as the standard treatment for symptomatic septal deviation, with high satisfaction and low complication rates in a 2022 narrative review.[18][19]

Freer describes submucous septal resection; Killian follows in 1904.[17]

lore.intro: Forum users discuss septoplasty mainly as a covered breathing operation and ask whether it can double as an aesthetic fix or be paired with other facial surgery.[4][5][6]

claims.claim: A functional septoplasty can be used to make small cosmetic changes to the nose, such as the tip.
claims.believers: One user planning an insurance-paid septoplasty asked how to persuade a surgeon to make small tip changes at the same time.[4]
claims.experts: Septoplasty is described as functional rather than cosmetic and distinct from rhinoplasty, which reshapes the external nose; combined septorhinoplasty is an established practice.[1][2]

claims.claim: Septoplasty alone may not straighten a crooked-looking nose, so some wait for or combine rhinoplasty or jaw surgery.
claims.believers: A poster asks whether to have rhinoplasty with their septoplasty or wait until after bimaxillary jaw surgery, which they believe could change the apparent size of the nose.[5]
claims.experts: Surgical literature distinguishes septal correction for airway function from external reshaping.[2][8]

claims.claim: Turbinate reduction risks empty nose syndrome.
claims.believers: A forum poster urges avoiding turbinate reduction altogether; another says it is the only fix for genuinely oversized turbinates.[10]
claims.experts: Wikipedia lists empty nose syndrome among reported complications of nasal surgery, and a larger body of ENT literature discusses turbinate surgery separately.[1]

claims.claim: Septoplasty is a stealth route to a better-looking nose when insurance pays.
claims.believers: Forum users with a covered breathing operation ask how to raise small tip adjustments with their surgeon at the same time.[4]
claims.experts: Wikipedia says septoplasty causes no cosmetic change, and describes cosmetic rhinoplasty as a separate operation done for aesthetic reasons.[16][17]

claims.claim: Septoplasty should be timed around jaw surgery.
claims.believers: Posters planning bimaxillary surgery ask whether to do septoplasty first or wait, because they expect jaw surgery to change how large the nose looks.[5][6]
claims.experts: A registered randomised trial examined functional nasal surgery at the time of Le Fort I jaw surgery; results are not described in the registry entry.[24]

chain: Straightens the cartilage and bone wall between the nostrils
Opens the airway and gives the nose a straighter internal frame
Can be paired with rhinoplasty so the outside of the nose is reshaped in the same operation
angle.text: Septoplasty is a breathing operation, and people who look into it for appearance usually do so because a bent septum can sit under a crooked-looking nose or supply cartilage for rhinoplasty. When looks are the goal, surgeons commonly combine it with rhinoplasty as septorhinoplasty so the inside and outside of the nose are addressed in one recovery.[1][16][17]
